claim: The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study is the largest and most comprehensive long-term study of brain development and child health in the United States.
source: The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) is the largest and most comprehensive long-term study of brain development and child health in the United States (Casey et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Casey et al., 2018

claim: The ABCD study includes 11,878 youth and their families.
source: The study includes 11,878 youth and their families and aims to understand the environmental, social, genetic, and other biological factors that affect brain and cognitive development.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the study composition

claim: CRAN granted $590 million in support to 21 research institutions across the United States to complete the ABCD study.
source: CRAN granted $590 million in support to 21 research institutions across the United States to complete this study.
evidence: Stated as a fact about funding

claim: The ABCD study includes three cognitive tasks during fMRI acquisition: the monetary incentive delay task, the emotional N-back task, and the stop-signal task.
source: The study organizers chose to include three cognitive tasks to be presented during fMRI acquisition: the monetary incentive delay task (Knutson et al., 2000), the emotional N-back task (Barch et al., 2013), and the stop-signal task (Logan and Cowan, 1984).
evidence: Stated as fact with citations to original task descriptions

claim: The authors analyzed behavioral data from the baseline scan of 8,464 of the 11,878 participants.
source: We analyzed behavioral data from the baseline scan of 8,464 of the 11,878 participants.
evidence: Stated as a description of the analysis sample

claim: The stop-signal task is a primary paradigm used to understand response inhibition.
source: The stop-signal task is a primary paradigm used to understand response inhibition.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about the stop-signal task

claim: The independent race model assumes that a go process begins when a go stimulus occurs and races independently against a stop process that begins when the stop stimulus occurs.
source: The dominant theoretical framework for understanding and interpreting stopping tasks is the independent race model (Logan et al., 2014; Logan and Cowan, 1984), which assumes that a go process begins when a go stimulus occurs and races independently against a stop process that begins when the stop stimulus occurs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Logan et al., 2014 and Logan and Cowan, 1984

claim: In the ABCD stop-signal task, 5/6 of all trials are go trials.
source: 5/6 of all trials are go trials, in which a subject sees a go stimulus (a rightward- or leftward-pointing arrow) and makes one of two speeded responses based upon the direction of the arrow.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: In the ABCD stop-signal task, the go stimulus is removed from the screen after 1000 ms or when a response occurs, whichever comes first.
source: The go stimulus is removed from the screen after 1000 ms or when a response occurs, whichever comes first.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: In the ABCD stop-signal task, on 1/6 of all trials, the go stimulus is replaced with the stop signal after the SSD or when a response occurs.
source: On 1/6 of all trials, this go stimulus is replaced with the stop signal (a vertical arrow) after the go stimulus has been on the screen for the duration of the SSD or when a response occurs; the stop signal is then presented for 300 ms (but see Issue 4).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: Mean go stimulus duration on go trials in the ABCD data was 569 ms (SD = 105 ms).
source: Mean go stimulus duration on go trials was 569 ms (standard deviation [SD] = 105 ms), and mean go stimulus duration on stop trials was 228 ms (SD = 118 ms), so on average, subjects had 341 ms longer on go trials to apprehend the go stimulus (see Figure 2 for full distributions).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data and shown in Figure 2

claim: Mean go stimulus duration on stop trials in the ABCD data was 228 ms (SD = 118 ms).
source: Mean go stimulus duration on go trials was 569 ms (standard deviation [SD] = 105 ms), and mean go stimulus duration on stop trials was 228 ms (SD = 118 ms), so on average, subjects had 341 ms longer on go trials to apprehend the go stimulus (see Figure 2 for full distributions).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data and shown in Figure 2

claim: The independent race model requires that the go process is the same on go and stop trials (context independence).
source: This is important because the current models for understanding stopping performance require that the go process is the same on go and stop trials.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the independent race model

claim: Context independence is essential for calculating SSRT because it allows one to assume that the full distribution of responses on go trials can stand in for the full distribution of go processes on stop trials.
source: Context independence is essential for calculating SSRT because context independence allows one to assume that the full distribution of responses on go trials can stand in for the (unobservable) full distribution of go processes on stop trials.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SSRT calculation

claim: Violations of context independence contaminate major dependent variables in the stop-signal task, including the inhibition function and stop-failure RT.
source: Additionally, violations of context independence contaminate other major dependent variables in the stop-signal task, including the inhibition function and stop-failure RT (Bissett et al., 2021; Logan and Cowan, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bissett et al., 2021 and Logan and Cowan, 1984

claim: Shorter duration stimuli yield slower responses in both simple and choice reaction times.
source: In both simple (e.g., Froeberg, 1907) and choice (e.g., Kaswan and Young, 1965) reaction times, there is evidence that shorter duration stimuli yield slower responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to Froeberg, 1907 and Kaswan and Young, 1965

claim: The effect of stimulus duration on response speed occurs even for stimuli presented for hundreds of milliseconds.
source: This effect of stimulus duration on response speed occurs even for stimuli presented for hundreds of milliseconds (Kahneman and Norman, 1964; Kaswan and Young, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kahneman and Norman, 1964 and Kaswan and Young, 1965

claim: Bloch's law states that intensity and duration can be traded off for shorter duration stimuli over the first 100 ms.
source: This relates to Bloch's law (Bloch, 1885), which states that intensity and duration can be traded off for shorter duration stimuli, though this trade-off only occurs over the first 100 ms.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bloch, 1885

claim: Pieron's law states that RTs decrease with stimulus intensity.
source: This also relates to Pieron's law, which states that RTs decrease with stimulus intensity (Pieron, 1914).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pieron, 1914

claim: In the ABCD dataset, mean stop-failure RT (M = 456 ms, SD = 109 ms) was shorter than overt responses on go trials (M = 543 ms, SD = 95 ms).
source: On average across all subjects, stop-failure RT (M = 456 ms, SD = 109 ms) was shorter than overt responses on go trials (M = 543 ms, SD = 95 ms, 95% confidence interval of the difference [85.9, 88.8]).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: For 524 of the 8,464 subjects (6.2%), mean stop-failure RT was longer than mean RT on overt responses in go trials.
source: However, for 524 of the 8,464 subjects (6.2% of all subjects), mean stop-failure RT was longer than mean RT on overt responses in go trials, suggesting that a subset of subjects violated context independence.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: Stop-failure trials in the ABCD data had much lower accuracy (79%) than overt go trials (90%).
source: Stop-failure trials had much lower accuracy (79%) than overt go trials (90%), 95% confidence interval of the difference (10.6%, 11.1%).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: Choice accuracy on stop-failure trials was increasingly impaired at shorter SSD.
source: Additionally, choice accuracy on stop-failure trials was increasingly impaired at shorter SSD (see Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3 from ABCD data

claim: In other datasets, choice accuracy on stop-failure trials, even at shorter SSDs, tends to be similar to overt go trials.
source: In other datasets, choice accuracy on stop-failure trials, even at shorter SSDs, tends to be similar to overt go trials (Bissett et al., 2021), which suggests that the impaired go accuracy on stop-failure trials in the present study results from the shorter go stimulus durations on stop trials in this task.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bissett et al., 2021

claim: All existing models for stopping assume that the parameters that generate the distribution of go processes take the same value on go and stop trials.
source: To our knowledge, all existing models for stopping assume that the parameters that generate the distribution of go processes take the same value on go and stop trials (e.g., Boucher et al., 2007; Logan et al., 2014; Logan et al., 2015; Matzke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple modeling papers

claim: There is no existing model that can capture the ABCD stopping data and no valid way to compute SSRT from these data because the go process is different on go and stop trials.
source: Therefore, there is no existing model that can capture the ABCD stopping data and no valid way to compute SSRT from these data because the go process is different on go and stop trials (see Figure 3).
evidence: Inferred from the combination of existing model assumptions and ABCD data characteristics

claim: Violations of context independence can occur even without Design Issue 1.
source: There is evidence that violations of context independence can occur even without the introduction of Design Issue 1 (Akerfelt et al., 2006; Bissett et al., 2021; Colonius et al., 2001; Gulberti et al., 2014; Ozyurt et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The violations in the ABCD dataset manifest in an unprecedented way (lower choice accuracy on stop-failure trials) that go beyond previous evidence for violations.
source: Second, as we mentioned above, the violations in the ABCD dataset manifest in an unprecedented way (i.e., lower choice accuracy on stop-failure trials) that go beyond previous evidence for violations (e.g., Bissett et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from comparison with previous literature

claim: The slowed go processing model would overestimate mean SSRT by 75 ms compared to the independent race model.
source: This would overestimate mean SSRT by 75 ms for the slower drift rate model (slower drift rate SSRT = 207 ms and independent race SSRT = 282 ms)
evidence: Result from simulation

claim: The mixture guessing model would underestimate SSRT by 61 ms compared to the independent race model.
source: underestimate SSRT by 61 ms with the mixture guessing model (mixture guessing = 343 ms)
evidence: Result from simulation

claim: The confusion model would overestimate mean SSRT by 22 ms compared to the independent race model.
source: and overestimate mean SSRT by 22 ms for the confusion model (confusion SSRT = 260 ms).
evidence: Result from simulation

claim: Nine percent of all stop trials in the ABCD data had an SSD of 0 ms.
source: Nine percent of all stop trials had an SSD of 0 ms (see Figure 6).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data and shown in Figure 6

claim: The stop success rate at 0 ms SSD in the ABCD data was 60.1%.
source: In these data, we found that the stop success rate at the 0 ms SSD was 60.1%.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: In the ABCD dataset, 2.7% of subjects had a coding error where all subsequent stop trials had a response erroneously recorded at the same timestamp after an initial fast response.
source: In the entire sample, only 2.7% of subjects had this specific problem.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: In the ABCD task, if SSD is ≤ 700 ms, then the stop signal is presented for 300 ms.
source: If SSD is ≤ 700 ms, then the stop signal is presented for 300 ms.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: In the ABCD task, if SSD is >700 ms, then the stop signal is presented for 1000-SSD.
source: If SSD is >700 ms, then the stop signal is presented for 1000-SSD, with a maximum SSD of 900 (and therefore a minimum stop duration of 100 ms).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: SSDs > 700 ms are rare in the ABCD data (1.1%).
source: SSDs > 700 ms are rare in these data (see Figure 6, 1.1%).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data and shown in Figure 6

claim: In the ABCD task, the probability of a stop signal given the immediately preceding trial was a stop signal is 0.
source: In the ABCD task, this value is 0, as stop trials never repeat.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: In the ABCD task, stop trials almost never occur if there was a stop trial two trials before (conditional probability of 1.8%).
source: Additionally, stop trials almost never occur if there was a stop trial two trials before (conditional probability of 1.8%).
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: Post-stop-signal slowing was around 20 ms for each quartile except the second, in which it was 40 ms.
source: This is not what we found (see Figure 8) as post-stop-signal slowing was around 20 ms for each quartile except the second, in which it was 40 ms.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data and shown in Figure 8

claim: 25,854 of the 376,479 trials (6.9%) classified as incorrect go trials appear to actually have the correct go response.
source: 25,854 of the 376,479 trials (6.9%) classified as incorrect go trials appear to actually have the correct go response.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: 61,215 of the 2,162,718 trials (2.8%) classified as correct go trials are incorrect go trials.
source: 61,215 of the 2,162,718 trials (2.8%) classified as correct go trials are incorrect go trials.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: 1,081 of the 260,053 trials (0.4%) classified as correct stops are incorrect stops, as they include one or more overt responses.
source: Finally, 1,081 of the 260,053 trials (0.4%) classified as correct stops are incorrect stops, as they include one or more overt responses.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: In the ABCD dataset, SSD starts at 50 ms.
source: In the ABCD dataset, SSD starts at 50 ms.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: The ABCD study uses a 0.167 stop probability.
source: This ABCD study uses a 0.167 stop probability, which is unusually low.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the task design

claim: Stop-signal probability is commonly 0.25, 0.33, or a similar value in stop-signal studies.
source: Stop-signal probability is commonly 0.25, 0.33, or a similar value in stop-signal studies (Verbruggen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verbruggen et al., 2019

claim: At least some of the ABCD design issues extend to the IMAGEN study.
source: We would also like to note that at least some of these design issues extend to the IMAGEN study (Schumann et al., 2010), which Garavan et al., 2020 note used 'A very similar task, with the same Go stimulus design features'.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with IMAGEN study description

claim: The authors' preliminary simulations suggest that mean SSRT estimates are contaminated by Design Issue 1 violations of context independence.
source: These preliminary simulations suggest that mean SSRT estimates are contaminated and individual differences may be contaminated by the Design Issue 1 violations of context independence, particularly if the true between-subject variability in SSRT is small.
evidence: Result from simulations

claim: Individual differences in SSRT may be contaminated by Design Issue 1 violations, particularly if the true between-subject variability in SSRT is small.
source: These preliminary simulations suggest that mean SSRT estimates are contaminated and individual differences may be contaminated by the Design Issue 1 violations of context independence, particularly if the true between-subject variability in SSRT is small.
evidence: Result from simulations

claim: If between-subject variability in SSRT is high (SD = 85 ms), rank correlations between alternative models and the independent race model are largely preserved (r range = 0.85–0.99, mean = 0.93).
source: If we assume high between-subject variability in SSRT (SD = 85 ms), then the rank correlations are largely preserved across generating models and SSD approaches (r range = 0.85–0.99, mean = 0.93).
evidence: Result from simulations shown in Table 1

claim: As between-subject variability in SSRT reduces to SD = 25 ms, rank correlations decrease (r range = 0.66–0.97, mean = 0.78).
source: However, as between-subject variability in SSRT reduces (SD = 25 ms), the rank correlations decrease (r range = 0.66–0.97, mean = 0.78).
evidence: Result from simulations shown in Table 1

claim: At very low between-subject variability (SD = 5 ms), rank correlations can become very low (r range = 0.18–0.89, mean = 0.63).
source: At very low between-subject variability, (SD = 5 ms) the rank correlations can become very low (r range = 0.18–0.89, mean = 0.63).
evidence: Result from simulations shown in Table 1

claim: At the limit of no between-subject variability in SSRT (SD = 0 ms), rank correlations remain well above 0 on average (r range = 0.02–0.91, mean = 0.54).
source: At the limit, if we assume no between-subject variability in SSRT and therefore between-subject variance is driven entirely by differences in SSD, go RT, and the different generating models, rank correlations continue to reduce but remain well above 0 on average (r range = 0.02–0.91, mean = 0.54).
evidence: Result from simulations shown in Table 1

claim: The eight design issues identified significantly compromise the utility of the stopping data in the ABCD study for understanding the construct of response inhibition.
source: Additionally, we believe that the most fundamental issues are incontrovertible errors, and in the aggregate, we believe these eight issues significantly compromise the utility of the stopping data in this study for understanding the construct of response inhibition.
evidence: Overall conclusion based on analysis of all issues

claim: Unless the ABCD community shows that Design Issue 1 does not distort conclusions based upon SSRT estimates, researchers should not use the ABCD dataset to estimate SSRTs.
source: Given the above empirical evidence and simulations, and as suggested by our reviewers, unless the ABCD community shows that this design issue does not distort conclusions based upon SSRT estimates (or any other stop-signal measure), researchers should not use the ABCD dataset to estimate SSRTs and should use the neuroimaging data with caution.
evidence: Recommendation based on analysis and simulations

claim: Researchers should use the ABCD neuroimaging data with caution.
source: Given the above empirical evidence and simulations, and as suggested by our reviewers, unless the ABCD community shows that this design issue does not distort conclusions based upon SSRT estimates (or any other stop-signal measure), researchers should not use the ABCD dataset to estimate SSRTs and should use the neuroimaging data with caution.
evidence: Recommendation based on analysis

claim: Removing stop trials with SSDs < 200 ms would remove 51.5% of all stop trials in the ABCD dataset.
source: However, note that removing stop trials that have SSDs < 200 ms would remove 51.5% of all stop trials in the ABCD dataset, leaving less than an average of 30 stop trials per subject.
evidence: Computed from ABCD data

claim: A rebuttal preprint manuscript has been submitted from a group of authors involved in the design of the ABCD stop-signal task.
source: Since the original submission of this manuscript, a rebuttal preprint manuscript has been submitted from a group of authors involved in the design of the ABCD stop-signal task (Garavan et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated as a fact about the publication history

claim: The rebuttal manuscript did not dispute the presence of any of the specific issues raised in this manuscript.
source: In short, we stand behind the conclusions of the present manuscript and found no evidence or argumentation within their rebuttal that meaningfully challenges any of our manuscript's conclusions; importantly, their manuscript did not dispute the presence of any of the specific issues raised below.
evidence: Stated as a fact about the rebuttal content

claim: The authors corrected an error in their code on July 17, 2020.
source: We would like to thank Garavan et al., 2020 for pointing out an error in our code, which we corrected on July 17, 2020 (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.05.08.084707v4).
evidence: Stated as a fact about code correction
